Evolutionary Learning AtlasPathogens organized by host effect
BP colors and exam-priority underlining retain their meanings. Blue items are learning concepts, pathogens/parasites and their treatment/prevention notes. Anti-infectives are categorized under Microbiology/Parasitology; noninfectious medicines remain under Pharmacology. Host-BP links indicate the stated direct mechanism, host-defense disturbance or tissue/inflammatory consequence, not a claim that every organism directly inhibits that BP. Treatment names are study associations, not interchangeable regimens; site, susceptibility and clinical setting matter.

Proposed prebiotic chemistry

Approximate age: ~4.4–4.0 Ga; candidate interval, not a dated origin

Environment: Young Earth: volcanic and hydrothermal chemistry, mineral surfaces and possible wet–dry cycles; little free oxygen and no modern ozone shield.

Major innovations: Candidate building-block synthesis, chemical energy coupling and molecular compartments; these are hypotheses, not established living systems.

Context sources: early life

Read each broad period through functional sets, useful sub-aspects and canonical BP mechanisms. The five personal abstractions are navigation lenses only; they do not assert containment, ancestry or a common mechanism.

Placements are broad working interpretations. “Provisional” marks candidate or reconstructed placements. Present-day anatomy is a learning reference, not evidence of ancient organs or machinery. Candidate prebiotic reactions do not establish whole-system self-maintenance or historical occurrence.

Bracket counts describe only the selected linked entries. “Part of” means mechanistic participation; “regulates” and “enables” express different relationships. Alternative mechanisms depend on context: homologous recombination and end joining apply to different repair situations; cytosolic and vacuolar cross-presentation are different antigen-processing routes.

LUCA

Approximate age: ~4.2–3.5 Ga; highly model-dependent, with one recent estimate near 4.2 Ga

Environment: Largely anoxic early oceans; redox gradients and microbial interactions; precise habitat remains disputed.

Major innovations: Shared genetic code, ribosomal translation, cellular energy conservation and core biosynthesis; LUCA was not the first life.

Context sources: early life

Diphtheria — eEF2 ADP-ribosylation inhibits host protein synthesis. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Diphtheria antitoxin plus penicillin or a macrolide, with airway assessment.

Diarrheagenic E. coli and Shigella — Shiga-toxin 28S rRNA depurination inhibits host protein synthesis. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Rehydration; selected Shigella infections receive an active antibiotic. Avoid routine antibiotics for suspected Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli.

Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter — Pseudomonas exotoxin A inhibits eEF2; this mechanism is not assigned to Acinetobacter. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility-directed antipseudomonal beta-lactams or other active agents. Acinetobacter requires its own susceptibility-directed approach; colistin is a selected-context agent.

Microbiology / antibacterials / aminoglycosides: Plazomicin — target bacterial 30S ribosomes; the Atlas translation BP is a cross-organism core.

Microbiology / antibacterials / tetracyclines: Omadacycline — target bacterial 30S ribosomes.

Microbiology / antibacterials / 50S inhibitors: Lefamulin — drug-specific inhibition of bacterial translation.

Bacteria

Approximate age: Early divergence after LUCA, broadly ~4.2–3.5 Ga; exact origin unresolved

Environment: Initially anoxic water and sediments; later expansion into illuminated, oxygenated and host-associated niches.

Major innovations: Bacterial envelope organization and metabolic diversification; oxygenic photosynthesis arose in particular later bacterial lineages.

Context sources: early life; oxygen history

Listeria — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ampicillin; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative in selected settings.

Nocardia — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; severe disease uses species- and susceptibility-directed combinations.

Brucella — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline plus rifampin or selected aminoglycoside-containing regimens.

Tularemia — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Gentamicin; selected contexts use doxycycline or ciprofloxacin.

Salmonella — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftriaxone or azithromycin in selected indications; uncomplicated nontyphoidal gastroenteritis often needs no antibiotic.

Legionella — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Azithromycin or levofloxacin in appropriate treatment regimens.

Tuberculosis — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Isoniazid, rifampin/rifabutin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol are core susceptible-TB study drugs; bedaquiline and other drugs have resistance-specific roles.

Leprosy — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Rifampin, dapsone and clofazimine in multidrug therapy.

Mycobacterium avium complex — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Macrolide plus ethambutol, with rifamycin in selected regimens.

Q fever — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline; chronic focal infection uses specialized combination regimens.

Candida — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Fluconazole in selected susceptible mucosal infections; echinocandins for many invasive contexts; amphotericin B in selected settings.

Cryptococcus — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amphotericin B plus flucytosine in induction regimens, followed by fluconazole in appropriate consolidation/maintenance treatment.

Aspergillus — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Voriconazole or isavuconazole; selected alternatives include amphotericin formulations.

Mucorales — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Liposomal amphotericin B with source control; posaconazole or isavuconazole in selected settings.

Histoplasma — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Itraconazole; amphotericin B for selected severe disease.

Talaromyces — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amphotericin B induction and itraconazole in appropriate regimens.

Leishmania — Intracellular survival or impaired host phagolysosomal clearance. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine or other species/site-specific agents; no single regimen covers every form.

Enterobacterales — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility- and site-directed beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, or other agents; selected ESBL infections use carbapenems. Diarrheagenic E. coli and Shigella — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Rehydration; selected Shigella infections receive an active antibiotic. Avoid routine antibiotics for suspected Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli.

Salmonella — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftriaxone or azithromycin in selected indications; uncomplicated nontyphoidal gastroenteritis often needs no antibiotic.

Campylobacter — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Azithromycin when antimicrobial treatment is indicated.

Helicobacter pylori — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Combination eradication therapy; bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole are key study associations. Regimen selection depends on resistance and prior exposure.

Candida — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Fluconazole in selected susceptible mucosal infections; echinocandins for many invasive contexts; amphotericin B in selected settings.

Giardia — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Tinidazole, metronidazole or nitazoxanide.

Trichomonas — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Metronidazole or tinidazole; partner treatment is a key study association.

Entamoeba — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Metronidazole or tinidazole for invasive disease, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin.

Cryptosporidium — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Nitazoxanide in selected immunocompetent cases; immune restoration is central in advanced HIV.

Cyclospora and Cystoisospora — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Balantioides — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Tetracycline or metronidazole in appropriate treatment contexts.

Trichuris — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole or mebendazole in appropriate regimens.

Fasciolopsis — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Praziquantel.

Capillaria — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole or mebendazole in appropriate regimens.

Adenovirus — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Usually supportive care; selected severe immunocompromised-host disease uses specialist antivirals.

Rhinovirus — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care; no routine pathogen-specific antiviral.

RSV and related respiratory viruses — Mucosal or epithelial injury with barrier dysfunction. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Mostly supportive care. Palivizumab is a retained preventive antibody study item, not routine treatment of established RSV disease.

Other herpesviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive or syndrome-specific care; HHV-8 disease management includes immune restoration and disease-specific therapy.

Adenovirus — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Usually supportive care; selected severe immunocompromised-host disease uses specialist antivirals.

Polyomaviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Immune restoration or adjustment of immunosuppression in the appropriate setting; no universal curative antiviral.

Poxviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Local/supportive care for molluscum; orthopoxvirus antivirals are indication- and guidance-specific.

Hepatitis B and D — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | HBV: tenofovir or entecavir in selected indications; HDV needs distinct management and is not automatically treated by HBV nucleos(t)ide suppression alone.

Hepatitis C — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Direct-acting combinations such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir; genotype, cirrhosis and prior treatment affect selection.

Enteroviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive and syndrome-specific care; polio vaccination is preventive.

Influenza — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Oseltamivir, zanamivir or baloxavir in appropriate indications.

Measles — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care and vitamin A in appropriate indications; vaccination is preventive.

Mumps and rubella — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care; vaccination is preventive.

RSV and related respiratory viruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Mostly supportive care. Palivizumab is a retained preventive antibody study item, not routine treatment of established RSV disease.

Coronaviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir in appropriate indications; supportive and immune-directed management depends on disease stage.

Dengue and yellow fever — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care; avoid assigning an unestablished routine pathogen-specific antiviral.

Neurotropic arboviruses — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive and syndrome-specific care; prevention varies by virus.

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care; specialist management for severe or immunocompromised-host infection.

HIV — Antiviral defense and viral immune-evasion context; the antagonist differs by virus. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Combination antiretroviral therapy; study classes include nucleos(t)ide RT inhibitors, non-nucleoside RT inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, protease inhibitors and selected entry inhibitors. Ritonavir/cobicistat are pharmacokinetic boosters in applicable combinations.

Staphylococcus aureus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | MSSA: nafcillin, oxacillin or cefazolin; selected MRSA contexts: vancomycin or linezolid, with daptomycin restricted to suitable nonpulmonary infections.

Streptococcus pyogenes — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Penicillin or amoxicillin; severe toxin-mediated disease: additional clindamycin.

Streptococcus agalactiae — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Penicillin or ampicillin; selected severe neonatal contexts include an aminoglycoside.

Pneumococcus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amoxicillin in susceptible contexts; ceftriaxone; vancomycin added in selected meningitis/resistance contexts.

Viridans and gallolyticus streptococci — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Penicillin or ceftriaxone according to susceptibility and syndrome.

Enterococci — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ampicillin when susceptible; vancomycin when appropriate; selected resistant infections: linezolid or daptomycin.

Bacillus cereus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Foodborne disease: supportive care; invasive infection: vancomycin or another active agent.

Clostridial myonecrosis — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Penicillin plus clindamycin in selected myonecrosis regimens; urgent source control.

Actinomyces — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Penicillin-class therapy; source control where indicated.

Nocardia — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; severe disease uses species- and susceptibility-directed combinations.

Meningococcus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftriaxone; exposure prophylaxis options include rifampin or other recommended agents.

Gonococcus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftriaxone; add chlamydia-directed treatment when indicated.

Haemophilus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftriaxone for selected invasive infections; amoxicillin/clavulanate in selected noninvasive settings.

Pasteurella — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amoxicillin/clavulanate in typical bite-wound contexts.

Brucella — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline plus rifampin or selected aminoglycoside-containing regimens.

Tularemia — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Gentamicin; selected contexts use doxycycline or ciprofloxacin.

Enterobacterales — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility- and site-directed beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, or other agents; selected ESBL infections use carbapenems. Nitrofurantoin is limited to suitable lower-urinary infections.

Yersinia — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Plague: gentamicin, doxycycline or a recommended alternative. Enterocolitis treatment depends on severity and susceptibility.

Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility-directed antipseudomonal beta-lactams or other active agents. Acinetobacter requires its own susceptibility-directed approach; colistin is a selected-context agent.

Vibrio vulnificus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline plus an appropriate third-generation cephalosporin in selected regimens; source control.

Helicobacter pylori — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Combination eradication therapy; bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole are key study associations. Regimen selection depends on resistance and prior exposure.

Legionella — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Azithromycin or levofloxacin in appropriate treatment regimens.

Anaerobic bacterial abscesses — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Metronidazole or an active beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor regimen, according to syndrome and source control.

Tuberculosis — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Isoniazid, rifampin/rifabutin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol are core susceptible-TB study drugs; bedaquiline and other drugs have resistance-specific roles.

Mycobacterium avium complex — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Macrolide plus ethambutol, with rifamycin in selected regimens.

Chlamydiae — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline; azithromycin in selected indications, including applicable pregnancy contexts.

Mycoplasma — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Macrolide or doxycycline according to context and resistance; beta-lactams lack a cell-wall target.

Rickettsial and related intracellular bacteria — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline is a core treatment association.

Q fever — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Doxycycline; chronic focal infection uses specialized combination regimens.

Spirochetes — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Syphilis: penicillin, with formulation determined by syndrome. Lyme disease: doxycycline/amoxicillin or selected ceftriaxone indications. Leptospirosis: doxycycline or selected parenteral beta-lactams.

Melioidosis — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ceftazidime or meropenem in intensive treatment; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in eradication treatment.

Bartonella — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Azithromycin or doxycycline-based treatment in selected syndromes.

Eikenella — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amoxicillin/clavulanate in typical bite-wound contexts.

Cryptococcus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amphotericin B plus flucytosine in induction regimens, followed by fluconazole in appropriate consolidation/maintenance treatment.

Aspergillus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Voriconazole or isavuconazole; selected alternatives include amphotericin formulations.

Mucorales — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Liposomal amphotericin B with source control; posaconazole or isavuconazole in selected settings.

Pneumocystis — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; selected alternatives include atovaquone or pentamidine.

Histoplasma — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Itraconazole; amphotericin B for selected severe disease.

Blastomyces — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Itraconazole or amphotericin B according to severity/site.

Coccidioides — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Fluconazole or itraconazole in selected indications; amphotericin B for selected severe cases.

Sporothrix — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Itraconazole; amphotericin B in selected severe/disseminated disease.

Talaromyces — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Amphotericin B induction and itraconazole in appropriate regimens.

Paracoccidioides — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Itraconazole; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a recognized alternative.

Trichomonas — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Metronidazole or tinidazole; partner treatment is a key study association.

Acanthamoeba — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Specialist combination therapy; biguanide-based topical therapy is an important keratitis association.

Toxoplasma — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin; spiramycin in selected pregnancy contexts.

Trypanosoma cruzi — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Benznidazole or nifurtimox.

Trypanosoma brucei — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Stage/species-specific therapy; retained study drugs include pentamidine, suramin, eflornithine, nifurtimox and melarsoprol. These are not interchangeable.

Naegleria — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Urgent specialist combination treatment; amphotericin B and miltefosine are key study associations.

Balantioides — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Tetracycline or metronidazole in appropriate treatment contexts.

Ascaris — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole or mebendazole.

Enterobius — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole, mebendazole or pyrantel pamoate.

Trichuris — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole or mebendazole in appropriate regimens.

Strongyloides — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ivermectin; albendazole is an alternative in selected settings.

Trichinella and Toxocara — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole or mebendazole in appropriate indications; inflammatory complications may need separate management.

Lymphatic filariae — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Diethylcarbamazine in appropriate individual-treatment contexts; region-specific programs and coinfections change drug selection.

Onchocerca — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Ivermectin; doxycycline targets Wolbachia in selected settings.

Loa loa — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Diethylcarbamazine; high-microfilarial-load management requires specialist selection.

Taenia solium — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Intestinal taeniasis: praziquantel or selected alternatives. Neurocysticercosis: lesion-specific albendazole/praziquantel and inflammatory management; not every lesion needs an antiparasitic.

Echinococcus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Albendazole; lesion-specific surgical or percutaneous management.

Schistosomes — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Praziquantel.

Liver flukes — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Praziquantel.

Fasciola — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Triclabendazole; do not generalize praziquantel to Fasciola.

Paragonimus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Praziquantel in appropriate treatment regimens.

Angiostrongylus and Gnathostoma — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Species- and site-specific specialist management. Albendazole/ivermectin are study associations for selected gnathostomiasis contexts; Angiostrongylus CNS disease is not assigned a universal antiparasitic regimen.

Ectoparasites — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Permethrin or other appropriate ectoparasiticides; ivermectin in selected scabies/lice contexts.

Dengue and yellow fever — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Supportive care; avoid assigning an unestablished routine pathogen-specific antiviral.

Hemorrhagic fever viruses — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Virus-specific supportive/specialist care; Ebola has species-specific antibody treatments, not a universal hemorrhagic-fever regimen.

Staphylococcus epidermidis — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility-directed treatment; vancomycin in selected resistant device-associated infections, with device/source management.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus — Pathological local or systemic inflammation and tissue injury. Full pathogen / treatment notes ↗ | Susceptibility- and site-directed therapy; nitrofurantoin is a study association for suitable S. saprophyticus lower-urinary infection.

Eutheria

Approximate age: ~160–125 mya for stem eutherians; crown placental radiation broadly ~100–66 mya

Environment: Jurassic–Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystems, followed by major ecological opportunities after the end-Cretaceous extinction.

Major innovations: Eutherian reproductive and placental specializations supporting prolonged gestation in many descendants; distinguish stem eutherians from crown Placentalia.

Context sources: therian/eutherian evidence; mammal timescales

Primates

Approximate age: ~70–55 mya for broad early primate evolution; clear euprimate fossils by ~56–55 mya

Environment: Predominantly wooded environments; branch-based locomotion and visually guided feeding in warm early Paleogene settings.

Major innovations: Grasping extremities, enhanced visual coordination and flexible arboreal behavior; individual traits have different evolutionary histories.

Context sources: early primates

Hominoidea

Approximate age: ~30–20 mya for stem ape divergence; later crown-ape diversification

Environment: Oligocene–Miocene African woodlands and forests, later extending into Eurasian habitats with changing seasonality.

Major innovations: Ape-lineage body-plan changes including tail loss and later trunk/shoulder specializations; suspension and large brains were not an original universal package.

Context sources: ape divergence

Functional set: Reproduction and early embryonic development

Build maternal–embryonic interfaces

BP - physiology: Syncytin-1–ASCT2-dependent trophoblast cell fusion <thymus, lymph nodes, spleen, peripheral tissues;lymphoid tissue; T lymphocyte, thymic epithelial cell, antigen-presenting cell>

Homo sapiens

Approximate age: ~0.3 mya to present

Environment: Variable African climates and habitats, followed by worldwide dispersal and increasingly human-modified environments.

Major innovations: A mosaic of modern human anatomy and expanded symbolic/cumulative cultural capacities; upright walking, tool use and sociality predate Homo sapiens.

Context sources: human origins

Organization notes and source checks

Core microbial cellular biology remains chronological. Pathogen inventories and disease mechanisms are organized by affected host functions. Broad or mechanical harm stays in General Pathogens/Parasites, at the former virus-section position. Its brackets link mapped BP entries; mechanical, vector-borne, nutritional and diffuse tissue effects are named explicitly. Antimicrobial facts that are shared across organisms remain in the Microbiology/Parasitology reference subsections there.

Existing numerical network relationships are retained as biochemical context, not reinterpreted as counts of infections. Original stable BP destinations and named bracket links remain navigable; a link to a moved pathogen mechanism now reaches its blue mechanism entry.

Source checks: CDC STI guidance; Strongyloides; schistosomiasis; Giardia; cryptococcosis; candidiasis; botulism; tetanus; malaria; scabies.

Pharmacology review: major examination domains and representative agents were cross-checked; this is not an inventory of every marketed drug. New underlined names indicate familiar study priority for either Taiwan’s first-stage physician examination or USMLE Step 1, not an official drug-frequency ranking.
